accepted.hypothesis: D15 has the strongest CO2 binding (-27.9 kcal/mol) and f=1.09, but a margin of -0.196. Monochlorination lowered the margin penalty only to -0.106 and cost little f (1.04), while dichlorination lowered f to 0.82. F is the halogen that raised f in the BQ series (F2 compound 1.65 vs Cl2 1.24), so one F on the ortho-quinone core should give a similar margin gain with a smaller f cost. The margin will probably stay below 0.15. This tests whether F is better than Cl on this core.

rejected.hypothesis: Replacing both Cl on D07 with F raised f from 1.24 to 1.65, so F is the f-promoting halogen. Here I take D08 (F4, f=1.03) and remove two F to give 2,5-difluoro-BQ, the para-disposed isomer of the 2,6-F2 compound. I expect f to rise as halogen count falls, as the D08 to trifluoro to F2 trend suggests. Margin should be near 0 to 0.1, so the margin is the risk. This tests whether the para arrangement lifts the margin without losing f. F4-BQ (K084) is a known CO2 adduct former.

rejected.hypothesis: Moving from Cl2 (f=1.24) to F2 gave f=1.65, and fewer halogens gave higher f (trifluoro 1.31 vs F4 1.03). Mono-fluoro-BQ pushes this to the limit and may reach f>=2 through strong CO2 binding, since the F2 compound bound at -28.3 kcal/mol. Margin will likely be negative, since the F2 compound dropped to -0.03. It tests the f end of the tradeoff, and DFT will decide whether f>=2 is reachable. The BQ core is a documented CO2 adduct former (K026).

rejected.hypothesis: The 2,6-F2 pattern gave the highest f (1.65) but its margin is -0.03. Br gave the largest margin (D11, 0.462), and adding Br at 3,5 on the Cl2 scaffold raised the margin to 0.40. It cut f to 0.72, but that was with two Br. Here only one Br is added to the F2 core, to raise the margin above 0.15 while most of the F-driven f is kept. This probes the margin gain per heavy halogen against the f loss.
